lessons.title: Building Models from Shapes

activities.prompt: How can we turn everyday shapes into models of buildings around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Models of Places
activities.body: Models help us show places and buildings. Diksha visited Delhi and saw the India Gate and Qutub Minar. Now she is making an India Gate model with wooden blocks. Qutub Minar is a World Heritage site. It is the tallest building made of bricks and has 5 storeys and 379 stairs. People also use boxes, bottles, cans and coconut shells for models.
keyPoints: Qutub Minar is a World Heritage site.
It has 5 storeys and 379 stairs.
Boxes, bottles, cans and coconut shells can help make models.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how people use shapes and materials to build models.

activities.prompt: How can Diksha turn her Delhi visit into models made from useful shapes?
steps: Her Delhi visit included India Gate and Qutub Minar.
She can use wooden blocks because India Gate is her model project.
Boxes, bottles, cans, and coconut shells can help make models.
So, Diksha can build models from shapes and useful materials.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

lessons.title: Making Nets, Prisms and Pyramids

activities.prompt: What might we create by folding flat paper into magical shapes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nets and Shape Models
activities.body: When Diksha folds open and flattens a box, the unfolded form is called its net. A net is the box’s open, flat shape. Folding the net along dotted lines gives the box back. The box returns to its earlier shape. Nets at the end of the book help us make models. The craft section groups the shapes under prisms and pyramids. We can make a sphere-like shape with paper strips.
keyPoints: Paper strips can make a sphere-like shape.
Models include a triangular prism and a triangular pyramid.
Models include a pentagonal pyramid and a square prism.
Models also include a square pyramid and a hexagonal prism.
activities.explanation: You have learned how nets help us make shape models.

activities.prompt: 4 paper strips make one sphere-like shape. How many strips are needed to make 2 sphere-like shapes?
steps: The given numbers are 4 strips for each shape and 2 shapes.
Each shape uses the same number of strips.
Multiply 4 by 2 because we need the total for all the shapes.
The answer is 8 strips.

activities.title: Look at the shape table
activities.body: Your book has a table for shapes. It records each shape's faces. It also records corners and edges. Here F means faces, V means corners and E means edges. You can look for a relationship between these counts. The formula F+V–E is calculated for each shape. Shapes can be sorted by their flat faces or straight edges. The flat-face groups include 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8.

activities.title: Different Views and Drawings
activities.body: Jagat asks the children to hide, and he will find them. Bholu is amazed by the tree from the top. Jagat takes a tree picture from the front. Top, front, and side views are kinds of views.
The same brick can have different drawings.
activities.explanation: This lesson explores hiding, different views, and different drawings.

activities.prompt: On the grid, Mini takes four steps right. Then Mini takes two left and one upward step. Where is Mini now?
steps: Each move counts, because players move up, down, left, or right.
Four right steps minus two left steps leave two steps right.
One upward step adds one step above the starting square.

lessons.title: Flying a Drone and Following a Sight Map

activities.prompt: How can a drone and a map help us find our way around school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Drone Pictures and Sight Maps
activities.body: A drone is a flying machine that can take pictures. Gyan shows her drone to her friends. The drone picture shows a school that looks green and beautiful. Its walls are made of red bricks. Preet’s elder sister has made a sight map. A sight map is a drawing that shows places and helps readers find them. This project begins at the school entrance.
keyPoints: A drone can take pictures while flying.
The school has walls made of red bricks.
A sight map shows places from the school entrance.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects drone pictures with places on a sight map.

activities.prompt: Gyan flies her drone on 2 trips, and it takes 2 pictures on each trip. How many pictures does her drone take in all?
steps: Gyan makes 2 trips, with 2 pictures taken on each trip.
Multiply the number of trips by the number of pictures per trip.
2 x 2 = 4 pictures in all.

gen.template: Gyan flies her drone on {flights} trips, and it takes {pictures} pictures on each trip. How many pictures does her drone take in all?
steps: Gyan makes {flights} trips, with {pictures} pictures taken on each trip.
Multiply the number of trips by the number of pictures per trip.
{flights} x {pictures} = {answer} pictures in all.
gen.hint: Count the pictures from each trip and combine all the trips.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: How can we draw a useful sight map from the school entrance?
steps: Start at the entrance because the project work must be drawn from there.
Use Preet’s elder sister’s sight map because it helps find Grade 4.
Include Bholu’s route because he must go to the IT room.
Include Rani’s route so the map helps her reach the sports room.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Can a Drone Do?
activities.prompt: What can a drone do while it is flying?

Make lunch
Wash clothes
Read books
activities.explanation: A drone can take pictures while it is flying.

activities.prompt: The water delivery man walks 3 steps from the entrance, then turns left and walks 3 more steps. How many steps does he walk in all?
activities.explanation: The first part of the route is 3 steps. The second part, after the left turn, is 3 steps. 3 + 3 = 6 steps in all.
steps: The first part of the route is 3 steps.
The second part, after the left turn, is 3 steps.
3 + 3 = 6 steps in all.
activities.hint: Add the steps from both parts of his route.

gen.template: The water delivery man walks {first} steps from the entrance, then turns left and walks {second} more steps. How many steps does he walk in all?
steps: The first part of the route is {first} steps.
The second part, after the left turn, is {second} steps.
{first} + {second} = {answer} steps in all.
gen.hint: Add the steps from both parts of his route.

activities.prompt: Preet's elder sister's sight map shows 7 places. One place is Grade 4. How many other places are on the sight map?
activities.explanation: There are 7 places on the sight map. Grade 4 uses one of those places, so remove that one place. 7 - 1 = 6 other places.
steps: There are 7 places on the sight map.
Grade 4 uses one of those places, so remove that one place.
7 - 1 = 6 other places.
activities.hint: Take away the one place marked Grade 4.

{places} - 1 = {answer} other places.

activities.explanation: Grade 4 can easily be found on the sight map.

activities.prompt: On Preet's elder sister's sight map, the school market is marked by 4 rows of 4 stalls. How many market stalls are marked on the sight map?
activities.explanation: The sight map has 4 rows of market stalls. Each row contains 4 stalls. 4 x 4 = 16 market stalls in all.
steps: The sight map has 4 rows of market stalls.
Each row contains 4 stalls.
4 x 4 = 16 market stalls in all.

activities.prompt: Two routes on the sight map lead from the entrance to the IT room. The shorter route is 7 steps long, and the longer route is 12 steps long. How many more steps is the longer route than the shorter route?
activities.explanation: The shorter route has 7 steps and the longer route has 12 steps. To find how many more steps the longer route has, subtract 7 from 12. 12 - 7 = 5 more steps.
steps: The shorter route has 7 steps and the longer route has 12 steps.
To find how many more steps the longer route has, subtract 7 from 12.
12 - 7 = 5 more steps.

why.The school looks green, and its walls ar: Its walls are red bricks, not green bricks.

Grade 4 is easy to find, but neither task ends there.

A drone picture is not the route from the entrance.

activities.context: Jagat tells all the children to hide, and he will find them. Bholu is amazed by how the tree looks from the top. Jagat takes a picture of a tree from the front. Mini, Bholu, and Rani all draw the same brick, but their drawings are different. They discuss why, and their teacher says that the children may give different answers. The teacher explains that top, front, and side views can all be discussed.
activities.prompt: If the three drawings of the same brick stay different, what is the best explanation?
options: They may have viewed the brick from different views.
They may have mistaken the brick for different objects.
They may have copied Jagat's tree picture.
They may all have used only the tree's front view.

why.They may have mistaken the brick for dif: The children are drawing the same brick.
why.They may have copied Jagat's tree pictur: They are drawing a brick, not a tree.
why.They may all have used only the tree's f: The children's activity does not involve Jagat's tree picture.

activities.explanation: Different views can produce different drawings of one brick.

activities.context: Jagat tells all the children to hide, and he will find them. Bholu is amazed by how the tree looks from the top. Jagat takes a picture of a tree from the front. Mini, Bholu, and Rani all draw the same brick, but their drawings are different. They discuss why, and their teacher says that the children may give different answers. The teacher explains that top, front, and side views can all be discussed.
activities.prompt: The teacher sees three different drawings of the same brick. What should the teacher do next?
options: Ask each child to explain which view they used.
Ask each child to make exactly the same drawing.
Choose one drawing and reject the others.
Ask each child to draw a tree instead.

why.Ask each child to make exactly the same: The teacher says that different answers may be given.
why.Choose one drawing and reject the others: The teacher should not reject different answers.
The activity is about drawing the same brick.

activities.explanation: Explaining the view helps the teacher understand the differences.

activities.prompt: How does a top view differ from a front view?
activities.answer: A top view is discussed when looking at an object from above it. A front view is discussed when looking at it from the front. That is why Bholu can be amazed by the top of the tree, while Jagat's picture shows the tree from the front.
points: Top means looking from above.
Front means looking from the front.
The two views show the object from different positions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Jagat and Mini empty a big bag of matchboxes onto the floor. Jagat stacks his boxes into a tall tower with a wide step at the bottom. Mini builds something lower, with a flat roof. Each of them walks around their own building and then sits down with paper and draws three pictures of that one building. When they finish, they swap their sheets.
activities.prompt: Mini's first picture shows one flat shape with no wall at all below it, only the outline of the roof. Which picture has she drawn?
options: the one taken by looking straight down at the building
the one taken by standing in front of the building
the one taken by standing behind the building
the one taken by crouching on the floor beside the building

why.the one taken by standing in front of th: A front picture would still show a wall standing below the roof.
why.the one taken by standing behind the bui: A back picture would also show a wall, not just a roof shape.
why.the one taken by crouching on the floor: Crouching beside the building still puts a wall in the way of the roof.

activities.explanation: Right — a flat roof seen from straight above hides the walls, so only the roof outline appears.

activities.context: Jagat and Mini empty a big bag of matchboxes onto the floor. Jagat stacks his boxes into a tall tower with a wide step at the bottom. Mini builds something lower, with a flat roof. Each of them walks around their own building and then sits down with paper and draws three pictures of that one building. When they finish, they swap their sheets.
activities.prompt: Jagat has only one sheet of Mini's building, the picture taken from the front. What can he NOT work out from that single picture?
options: how far the roof stretches towards the back
how wide the front of the building is
how tall the front of the building is
how many boxes sit in the front row

why.how wide the front of the building is: The width across the front is exactly what a front picture shows.
why.how tall the front of the building is: The height of the front is also shown in a front picture.
why.how many boxes sit in the front row: Boxes along the front row can be counted in a front picture.

activities.explanation: Right — reaching back away from the viewer is hidden in a front picture.

activities.prompt: Explain why Jagat and Mini draw the same building three times instead of only once.
activities.answer: A single drawing shows only one side of a building, so the parts behind it stay hidden. The front, back and top pictures each show something the others hide, and together they give the shape of the whole building.
points: one drawing shows only one side
each view hides something the other views show
three views together describe the whole building
all the drawings are of the same building
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How does the cat’s position help it find Jagat?
activities.answer: The cat is sitting on the window and trying to find Jagat. Since Jagat is at the third desk in the first row, the cat should look in that part of the classroom. This uses Jagat’s known position instead of searching other desks.
points: The cat is sitting on the window.
The cat is trying to find Jagat.
Jagat is at the third desk.
Jagat’s desk is in the first row.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Jagat thinks of the hidden object while Mini searches for it on a four-by-four grid. Mini first takes four steps to the right, then takes two steps to the left and one step upwards. The player is still two steps away. Mini and Jagat trace paths, count the steps, and use only up, down, left, or right movements. They cannot move diagonally. The flower, mango, or orange may be the destination.
activities.prompt: Mini is still two steps away. What should Mini do next?
options: Continue tracing an allowed path until the hidden object is reached.
Make a diagonal move directly toward the hidden object.
Jump to the destination without counting any more steps.
Stop tracing because the object is no longer hidden.

why.Make a diagonal move directly toward the: This mistake breaks the rule against diagonal movement.
why.Jump to the destination without counting: This mistake skips the required tracing and counting.
why.Stop tracing because the object is no lo: This mistake treats being close as if the object had been found.

activities.explanation: Correct: This keeps the search on an allowed path.

activities.context: Jagat thinks of the hidden object while Mini searches for it on a four-by-four grid. Mini first takes four steps to the right, then takes two steps to the left and one step upwards. The player is still two steps away. Mini and Jagat trace paths, count the steps, and use only up, down, left, or right movements. They cannot move diagonally. The flower, mango, or orange may be the destination.
activities.prompt: Jagat changes the hidden destination from the mango to the orange. What should Mini do next?
options: Continue with vertical or horizontal steps along a new path to the orange.
Use a slanting step to the orange because destinations can change.
Change to a larger grid because the destination changed.
Stop counting the route because the destination changed.

why.Use a slanting step to the orange becaus: This mistake wrongly allows diagonal movement.
why.Change to a larger grid because the dest: This mistake wrongly changes the four-by-four grid.
why.Stop counting the route because the dest: This mistake wrongly stops the counting of path steps.

activities.explanation: Correct: The movement rules stay the same while the path changes.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between moving right and moving up.
activities.answer: Moving right means Mini goes sideways on the grid. Moving up means Mini goes vertically on the grid. Both movements are allowed and count as one step. Neither is diagonal because a diagonal movement changes sideways and upward at the same time.
points: Identifies right as a sideways movement.
Identifies up as a vertical movement.
States that both movements are allowed.
Explains that neither movement is diagonal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a drone picture and a sight map for this school project.
activities.answer: A drone picture shows that the school looks green and beautiful and that its walls are made of red bricks. A sight map helps people find places, and Grade 4 can easily be found on Preet’s elder sister’s map. The project is to draw a sight map from the entrance.
points: A drone takes pictures while flying.
The picture shows the school’s green and beautiful appearance.
The picture shows walls made of red bricks.
A sight map helps people find places such as Grade 4.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: Even and Odd Patterns
activities.body: Even and odd numbers are two ways to sort numbers. Shiv has arranged his numbers in pairs. Numbers that can be paired are called even numbers. Shirley’s numbers are called odd numbers. You can draw the pairing arrangement. Objects that can be paired show the even pattern. Objects that cannot be paired show the odd pattern.

Shirley’s numbers are odd.
Pairing arrangements can be drawn.
activities.explanation: Pairs help you spot the even pattern.

activities.context: A club is preparing a display about large numbers. The children have practised writing from 1 to 999, and their teacher says the lesson now begins with 1000 and larger numbers. activities.prompt: If the club adds another number after 1100, what should it do?

why.Restart from 1 because the system cannot: This wrongly assumes that the system cannot handle numbers above 999.
why.Replace each number with a new symbol be: This wrongly assumes that larger numbers cannot be written with the same symbols.

activities.explanation: The system can write numbers of any size, so the list should continue.

activities.title: Learn about equal parts
activities.body: One half means each of two equal parts. One quarter means each of four equal parts. If an object is divided into five equal parts, each part is one-fifth. Two quarters together make the same amount as one half. A rectangle can be folded or cut in different ways to make two equal parts. It can also be cut into four equal parts.
keyPoints: A half is one of two equal parts.
A quarter is one of four equal parts.
Two quarters together equal one half.
activities.explanation: Equal parts help us name and compare shares.

activities.prompt: Ikra has 12 equal marbles. She gives Samina one half. How many marbles does Samina get?
steps: Ikra has 12 equal marbles.
One half means dividing them into 2 equal groups, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
Samina gets 6 marbles.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us observe: length and its words; measuring is fun; let us think: guess the length; measuring small things.

lessons.title: Let Us Observe: Length and Its Words

activities.prompt: Which words tell us about length, and when do we use each one?

activities.title: Words for Length
activities.body: Length means how long, tall, wide or deep something is. In this lesson, you will use the metre to measure length. You will also meet words such as height, width, depth and breadth. These words all describe length measurement. Sometimes, a word depends on the situation and how an object is placed. You will practise choosing and using length words.
keyPoints: Lengths are measured in metres.
Height, width, depth and breadth describe length measurement.
Length words depend on the situation and orientation.
activities.explanation: The metre measures length, and the lesson words describe different length measurements.

activities.prompt: A toy train track is 3 metres long. How many metres longer than one metre is it?
steps: The toy train track is 3 metres long.
We need to find how much longer it is than one metre.
Subtract one metre from its length: 3 - 1 = 2 metres.
The answer is 2 metres.

activities.title: Measuring with Ropes

The child with the greatest jump is found. Children also estimate their classroom's length and breadth, then check.

Ropes measure long jumps and classroom sizes.

activities.title: What is perimeter?
activities.body: Perimeter is the length of a shape’s boundary. A boundary is the edge around a closed figure. You can measure perimeter with informal units, such as footsteps, thumbprints or block printing. Formal measurements are more accurate. A scale or measuring tape helps you measure carefully. Dot grids with 1 cm spaces can also help you find perimeter.

activities.title: Remembering weight
activities.body: In Grade 3, we learnt to measure things. The examples were a 1-kilogram salt packet and a 1-litre bottle. One 500-gram packet is half a kilogram. Shabnam went to a market, where a vegetable seller weighed vegetables. We check weight guesses with a weighing balance. We write kg for kilogram and g for gram. Two 500-gram packets make 1 kilogram. Weights can be less than or more than 1 kilogram.

kg means kilogram and g means gram.
One 500-gram packet is half a kilogram.

lessons.title: Reverse and Add

activities.prompt: What happens when we turn a number backward and add it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reverse and Add
activities.body: Start with a two-digit number. Reverse its digits to make another number. Then add the original number and its reversed number. For example, 27 becomes 72, and their sum is 99. You can use this method with different two-digit numbers. You can also check whether a three-digit sum is possible.
keyPoints: Reverse the digits.
Add the number and its reverse.
Check whether a three-digit sum is possible.
activities.explanation: Reversing and adding helps you find special sums.

activities.prompt: A child at school starts with 27. What should the child do to use reverse-and-add?
steps: Start with 27 because the example begins with it.
Reverse its digits to make 72 because the digits change order.
Add 27 and 72 because the method pairs a number with its reverse.
The result is 99, so reverse-and-add gives 99 for 27.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Checking Reverse-and-Add Sums
activities.body: You can use the reverse-and-add method with different two-digit numbers. Some numbers belong on the 55-list or the 88-list. These lists group numbers by the sum made with their reverse. You can also check whether a three-digit sum is possible. The smallest possible three-digit sum is another question to solve.
keyPoints: Use different two-digit numbers.
Check the sum made with each reverse.
Look for the smallest possible three-digit sum.
activities.explanation: Different sums need different lists and checks.

activities.explanation: The digits of 27 are reversed to make 72.

activities.prompt: Adding 27 and its reverse makes 99.
activities.explanation: Yes. The reverse of 27 is 72, and 27 + 72 makes 99.

activities.title: Find the Sum
activities.prompt: Adding 27 and its reverse makes ______.
activities.hint: Reverse 27 first.
activities.explanation: The reverse is 72. Adding 27 and 72 makes 99.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the example to its result.
activities.explanation: The example starts with 27, reverses it to 72, and adds them to make 99.

activities.prompt: The lesson also asks for the ______ possible three-digit sum.
activities.hint: Find the sum that is not larger than others.
activities.explanation: The smallest possible three-digit sum is also asked for.

activities.title: Order the Steps
activities.prompt: Put the reverse-and-add steps for 27 in order.
activities.explanation: Start with 27, reverse it to 72, then add the two numbers to make 99.

options: 27 and 27

why.27 and 27: This uses 27 twice and forgets to reverse it.
why.72 and 72: This uses 72 twice and forgets to keep 27.
why.27 and 99: This adds the finished sum instead of the reversed number.

activities.explanation: Reversing 27 gives 72, and adding them gives 99.

options: Add only 27 and 99.
Add 27 and 72 again.
Add only 27 and 72.
Add only 72 and 99.

This adds the original number to the finished sum.
This repeats the correct addition instead of choosing the pair.
This adds the reversed number to the finished sum.

activities.explanation: Reverse-and-add uses the starting number and its reverse.

activities.prompt: Two lists hold reverse-and-add results. One is for 55, and one is for 88. Where does 99 belong?
options: In the 55 list
In the 88 list
In both lists
In neither list

why.In the 55 list: A number in the 55 list must have a sum of 55.
why.In the 88 list: A number in the 88 list must have a sum of 88.
why.In both lists: One sum cannot be both 55 and 88 at the same time.

activities.explanation: The sum for 27 is 99, which is neither 55 nor 88.

activities.prompt: Two lists contain sums of 55 and 88. Can those lists alone show a three-digit sum is possible?
options: No, because 55 and 88 have two digits.
No, because reverse-and-add never makes three-digit sums.
Yes, because 55 and 88 are larger than zero.
Yes, because every reverse-and-add sum has three digits.

activities.explanation: The two lists show only the two-digit sums 55 and 88.

lessons.title: Catty Wall and Nature Walk

activities.prompt: Can you make a cat from paper and find symmetry in nature?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Make and explore
activities.body: Start a catty wall with a square piece of paper. Mark the cat’s head and ears. Slide the top piece down to align it with the larger piece. The catty-wall tiles fit perfectly without gaps or overlaps. Fallen leaves can look symmetrical, and the butterfly looks symmetrical. On a nature walk, collect leaves, petals and flowers. Put leaves into symmetrical and non-symmetrical groups. Make designs, patterns, a greeting card and animals.
keyPoints: A square piece of paper starts the catty wall.
The top piece slides down to align with the larger piece.
Fallen leaves and the butterfly show symmetry.
Leaves and flowers can make many creations.
activities.explanation: This lesson joins paper folding, symmetry and nature.

activities.prompt: On a nature walk, 14 leaves are placed in a tray, and 8 of them look symmetrical. How many leaves are not symmetrical?
steps: There are 14 leaves altogether, and 8 look symmetrical.
Subtract 8 from 14 to count the leaves that are not symmetrical.
6 = 6 leaves.

activities.context: A learner is making an ink design for a school activity. First, the learner folds a sheet of paper in half. Once the design is finished, the learner looks at it and checks whether it is symmetrical by finding a line that divides it into two equal halves.
activities.prompt: Before pressing the paper, where should the learner put the drops of water colours?
options: Away from the folded edge
At the middle of the folded edge
At one corner of the sheet
Along the outer edge only

why.Away from the folded edge: The colours must be at the centre of the fold.
why.At one corner of the sheet: A corner is not in the centre of the fold.
why.Along the outer edge only: The outer edge is not the centre of the fold.

activities.explanation: This follows the first steps for making the ink design.

The design passes the symmetry check.

The design cannot be checked for symmetry.

Finding an equal-halves line shows that the symmetry check is successful.
The colours have already been placed and spread evenly.
why.The design cannot be checked for symmetr: An equal-halves line allows the design to be checked for symmetry.

activities.explanation: The folding step has already been completed.

Water colours are placed at the centre of the fold.
Pressing makes the colour spread evenly.
The finished design is checked for a line giving two equal halves.

Mark lines of symmetry in Figures 3, 4 and 5.
Count the lines of symmetry in Figure 8.
Make another airplane without symmetry before comparing anything.

why.Mark lines of symmetry in Figures 3, 4 a: Marking lines in Figures 3, 4 and 5 is a separate task.
Counting the lines in Figure 8 does not check the reflection.
why.Make another airplane without symmetry b: Making another airplane would skip the comparison.

Copy the shape once without comparing its sides.

why.Draw a reflection line even though the o: A reflection line is correct only when the opposite sides match.

lessons.title: The Transport Museum and Multiples of 100

activities.prompt: How many children can ride the museum’s toy train, and any left over?

activities.title: A Visit to the Transport Museum
activities.body: The Transport Museum collects different modes of transport, including vehicles from the olden days. Its toy train has fifteen coaches, and each coach seats fourteen children. So fifteen times fourteen equals two hundred ten. When three hundred twenty-four children are divided by fourteen, two remain. The number left over is called a remainder. Multiples of one hundred include two hundred and one thousand. They also include one thousand one hundred and two thousand.
keyPoints: The museum collects different modes of transport.
The toy train can seat two hundred ten children.
A remainder is the number left over after division.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect the museum, the toy train, remainders, and multiples of one hundred.

activities.prompt: The toy train has fifteen coaches. Each coach seats fourteen children. How many children can sit in the whole train?
steps: Each coach can seat fourteen children, so each coach gives one group of fourteen.

Multiplying counts all the groups, and fifteen times fourteen equals two hundred ten.
So, two hundred ten children can sit in the toy train.

activities.title: Travel Around India
activities.body: Travel can involve trains, buses and boats. The Punjab Mail is the Indian Railways' oldest long-distance train. It first travelled on 12 October 1912. A sightseeing bus seats two people per seat. It has fifteen lower-deck seats and ten upper-deck seats. Tickets and journeys have different prices. A brick kiln makes bricks for sale. Chilika lake in Odisha is India's largest saltwater lake. An amusement-park ticket costs ₹750.
keyPoints: The Punjab Mail first travelled on 12 October 1912
The sightseeing bus seats two people per seat
Chilika lake is India's largest saltwater lake
activities.explanation: These examples show how trains, buses, boats and tickets are described.

activities.prompt: A sightseeing bus has 5 lower-deck seats. Each seat can hold 2 people. How many people can sit on the lower deck?
steps: There are 5 lower-deck seats.
